summary:
Kabardino-Balkaria stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect. The Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation and the expanded propaganda statute, which reaches any public expression justifying gender transition, apply in every region of the country. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers so.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Kabardino-Balkaria, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. In this region, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are assessed as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns running from 2017 to 2024, and records that the 2023 extremist designation exposes LGBT+ activity to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. Working in exile, Isteev attests that conditions in the region deteriorate year on year.

For a trans visitor, the operative risk in Kabardino-Balkaria is therefore the regional one layered on top of the national statutes: security structures applying an extremist designation to any visible LGBT+ presence, in a territory where the state's own asylum authority assesses persecution as likely rather than merely possible.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume nationally has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two preceding years.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, under both administrative and criminal provisions, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation.

Coercive practices against trans people are documented at national scale. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kabardino-Balkaria cannot obtain legal gender recognition or access gender-affirming care anywhere in Russia, since the 2023 statute prohibits both gender reassignment surgery and changes to gender markers on official documents.

Public expression falling within the expanded propaganda provisions, including anything justifying gender transition, is criminalised, and LGBT+ organising is exposed to six to ten years' imprisonment under the extremist designation, with two to six years for lesser participation.

The UK Home Office note of June 2025 affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims; for residents of this republic the same note applies the higher persecution finding.

North Caucasus SOS reports that families themselves are a vector of risk, with detention and forced return to relatives among the outcomes facing LGBTIQ+ people whose existence becomes known, and that the trajectory in the region worsens annually.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kabardino-Balkaria-specific statute, decree or enforcement action targeting trans people appears in the source inventory; the republic-level picture rests on the regional assessment in the UK Home Office note and the testimony of North Caucasus SOS, and any local instrument would need separate verification.

The inventory documents no trans-specific violent incident, detention or killing inside Kabardino-Balkaria itself. The dated incidents cited here occurred elsewhere in Russia, and the 2017–2024 campaigns are recorded at regional rather than republic level.

Whether local security services in this republic have pursued extremism charges under the 2023 designation, and at what volume, is not sourced. Nor is there information on document checks at airports or checkpoints, on local access to ID correction, or on the availability of competent medical care for trans visitors.

The date on which the UK Home Office country policy note was last page-updated is recorded as 12 August 2026 in the source material; the substantive content cited is the June 2025 version.
